title: A Tiny Motor Inspired by an Ancient Screw
summary:
Scientists have built a remarkable molecular motor that spins when electricity passes through it and reverses direction when the voltage is switched.

Nature already has molecular motors inside living cells, and researchers have spent decades trying to copy them, work recognized with the 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The first electricity-powered molecular motors, built in 2011, sat on surfaces and relied on a scanning tunneling microscope tip to drive them.

The new motor borrows its design from the Archimedes screw, one of the oldest machines in recorded history. Traditionally used to move water uphill, it uses a rotating spiral to transport material. Here, electrons travel through a spiral-shaped molecule, and their flow makes the molecule rotate.

The spiral molecule, created by Prof. Michael Pittelkow's group at the University of Copenhagen, measures only a few millionths of a millimeter and attaches to gold through sulfur atoms. At Israel's Weizmann Institute, Prof. Oren Tal and Dr. Anil Kumar Singh placed molecules between two atomically sharpened gold tips, stretching or compressing the screw by changing the gap.

When voltage was applied, the molecule rotated, and reversing the voltage's polarity reversed its direction: the first current-driven molecular motor firmly connected to two metal electrodes with controllable direction. Electrons transfer angular momentum to the spiral as they pass, like moving air turning a wind turbine, and above a voltage threshold rotation becomes continuous.

Rotation brought a surprise: the spinning molecule conducted electricity far better than when still. Simulations by Prof. Fabian Pauly and PhD students Léon Martin and Yuta Ito at the University of Augsburg, run on the LiCCA supercomputer, showed conductivity rising by as much as 100 times during rotation. The positions that conduct best are ones the molecule naturally avoids at rest, Martin explained: only rotation makes them accessible.
why_it_matters: Machines this small could one day power tiny devices, and this motor shows how an ancient idea can solve a modern engineering puzzle.
